storm.summary_layperson: Radar is clear over the cove right now and no thunderstorms are expected tonight, but a Flood Watch is in effect for the region through Sunday afternoon ahead of a wet system moving in overnight — the cove has no cooling-water buffer against it tonight since the Sound and the air are nearly the same temperature.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Air-water gap is only about 1°F right now, already below the 5°F threshold for a stabilizing marine layer, so the cove gets no protective or amplifying effect from the Sound tonight — it will see the same conditions as the surrounding coast.
storm.detail_html:
Radar out of KOKX shows no storm cells anywhere near the cove as of 3:52 PM, and modeled instability (CAPE) is sitting at 0 J/kg for the evening hours. There is no active convective threat for the 5–10 PM window itself.

The region is under a Flood Watch issued by NWS Upton at 3:05 PM, running through Sunday at 2:00 PM. The Saturday-evening Area Forecast Discussion points to a slow-moving system bringing heavy showers and a few thunderstorms overnight into Sunday, with model soundings showing MLCAPE building to 500–1,000 J/kg over the Connecticut coast and Long Island by early Sunday morning, plus slow upshear steering that favors storms training over the same areas (backbuilding) and raises the flash-flood risk.

The cove's usual defense against incoming storms is a stable marine layer — cool Sound water sitting under warmer air, which can choke off low-level instability. That mechanism isn't available tonight: the air–water gap is already down to about 1°F this afternoon, well under the ~5°F threshold needed for a meaningful buffer, and it stays negligible (even reversing slightly, air cooler than water) for the rest of the evening. So tonight the cove won't see any extra shielding — or any extra punch-through risk — relative to inland Riverside or Stamford.

Most likely outcome for the 5–10 PM window: dry and quiet, consistent with current radar and zero CAPE. The real risk window is overnight into Sunday morning, outside tonight's forecast window, driven by the frontal/moisture setup described in the AFD rather than anything happening at the cove right now. What would change this call: any earlier-than-expected destabilization showing up on radar before midnight, or the AFD's onset timing shifting earlier.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light gradient wind with no sea breeze in play — expect 6-10 kt settling SSE through the evening, with pressure favoring the right side of the beat toward Belle Haven/Field Point. Play it cautious: direction has been wandering, not oscillating cleanly.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today is a gradient-only day (internally, B-light): the air–water temperature difference is just 0.7°F, far short of the 5°F needed to build a sea breeze, so nothing thermal is driving this wind — it's straight synoptic flow. The well-sited station average (KBDR/KHPN/KHVN etc.) puts the gradient at 7.4 kt, and direction agreement across the station network is weak (0.66), both of which point to the lighter B-light sub-case rather than a solid moderate breeze.

Current flow is out of the SSE-SE quadrant. Per the cove's geography, SSE flow gets partially sheltered by Greenwich Point (Tod's Point), leaving the east side of the course lighter and shiftier — pressure favors the west shore near Belle Haven and Field Point, which on a beat with the wind from this quadrant means favoring the right side.

Shift character here is more "wandering" than clean oscillation or a persistent frontal shift. HRRR itself shows the direction sliding from ESE early in the window to SSE by 7 PM and backing again toward 8 PM, and there's a real divergence between RYC (ESE at 3.8 kt) and the western-Sound station ensemble (SSE at 4.2 kt) — about 40° apart. Both readings are light, so this looks like normal local eddying in weak gradient flow rather than a boundary or front moving through.

On the water, 6-10 kt is the sweet spot for one-design dinghies for most of the window, easing toward 7-8 kt with lighter gusts by 9-10 PM. Note that HRRR model data only extends to 8 PM tonight (later forecast hours failed to fetch) — the 9 PM and 10 PM figures above are persistence-based extrapolations of the established light-SSE trend, not direct model output, so treat the back half of the window with lower confidence. No backdoor cold front risk tonight: the deltaT gate (5°F) isn't met, so the three-condition backdoor trigger can't fire regardless of the upstream KBOS/KPVD readings.
